Text
Matching the Topic. The passage tells the story of Mark’s trip to a little, previously‑unvisited island and describes his experiences, which fits the prompt “a story about an unusual holiday trip”. 5/5
Logic & Commonsense. The narrative contains a few oddities (e.g., “intelligent” locals, the sudden magical tone) that strain realism, but overall the events follow a coherent, if whimsical, storyline. 3/5
Vocabulary & Grammar. Most sentences are grammatical, but there are awkward phrasings (“intelligent in a strange way”, “He didn’t.”) and minor lexical mismatches. 3/5
---
Q1
Logic & Commonsense. The question asks for the reason Mark was nervous, which is a sensible detail to query. 4/5
Vocabulary & Grammar. The sentence is clear and correctly formed. 5/5
Text-Based Answerability. The text states “no one had visited the island before,” providing the needed information. 5/5
Reading Dependency. A test‑taker could guess that nervousness stems from the island being unknown, but the exact wording isn’t obvious without reading. 3/5
Answer Unambiguity. Only one option matches the text; the distractors are clearly different. 5/5
Distractor Plausibility. “Afraid of the locals” and “didn’t like strange food” are plausible misunderstandings; “too lazy to travel” is weaker but still a possible misinterpretation. 4/5
Using Paraphrases. The correct answer (“He had never heard of the island before”) paraphrases the text’s “no one had visited the island before.” 4/5
Explanation Quality. The explanation accurately links the correct answer to the passage and shows why each distractor is inconsistent. 5/5
---
Q2
Logic & Commonsense. Asking what purchase made Mark happy is a natural comprehension check. 5/5
Vocabulary & Grammar. The question is well‑phrased and free of errors. 5/5
Text-Based Answerability. The passage explicitly says he bought a hat that made him happy. 5/5
Reading Dependency. While “hat” is a likely guess, a test‑taker could also imagine other items; the answer isn’t obvious without the text. 3/5
Answer Unambiguity. Only “A colorful hat” fits the description; other choices are clearly unrelated. 5/5
Distractor Plausibility. “Intelligent book” feels forced, “Strange fruit” is plausible because fruit appears later, and “Polite souvenirs” is marginally plausible. Overall, distractors are uneven. 3/5
Using Paraphrases. The correct answer repeats the word “hat” directly from the text rather than paraphrasing it. 3/5
Explanation Quality. The explanation correctly points out the textual evidence and why each distractor is inappropriate. 5/5
---
Q3
Logic & Commonsense. It is reasonable to wonder why the boy warned Mark; the answer invokes danger, which aligns with common sense. 4/5
Vocabulary & Grammar. The question is grammatically sound. 5/5
Text-Based Answerability. The passage only gives the warning (“Don’t eat it!”) without stating the boy’s reasoning, so the answer requires inference beyond the explicit text. 3/5
Reading Dependency. A test‑taker could guess that a warning implies danger, making the correct answer moderately guessable. 4/5
Answer Unambiguity. Because the text does not state the boy’s motive, the “magical and dangerous” answer is not the sole logical inference, leaving some ambiguity. 3/5
Distractor Plausibility. All three distractors are conceivable misinterpretations, though “the boy was lazy” is less believable. 4/5
Using Paraphrases. The correct answer is phrased in new wording, not a verbatim lift from the passage. 5/5
Explanation Quality. The explanation ties the answer to the magical‑island theme but overstates what the text actually says; it could be tighter about the lack of explicit justification. 3/5
---
Text Coverage. The three items probe distinct sections: nervousness (opening), market purchase (middle), and fruit warning (later), ensuring broad coverage of the narrative. 5/5
